headline: Why did the bass suddenly commit? Ask the bunker off Brigantine
subhead: The new moon tide finally squeezed bait tight to the beach — here's the rundown on what that's changing and what to fish for it.
body_markdown:
Here's a question I got three different versions of at the tackle counter this week: why did the stripers go from picking at stragglers to actually eating, almost overnight? The short answer is the calendar. The new moon on the 10th delivered the strongest tidal push we've seen since spring, and that kind of current does one thing very reliably — it squeezes bunker schools tight against structure. Beaches, inlet mouths, jetty rocks. When bait gets pinned like that, predators stop being polite about it.

We flagged this exact pattern last week — said to watch the peanut bunker working down the beach as the tripwire for both surf bass and blitzing blues, and that's precisely what's unfolding from Brigantine down through Absecon Inlet and out past Great Egg. The bait isn't just present anymore, it's compressed, and compressed bait under a building moon is the first real feeding commitment of the fall run. Not the whole run — just the opening bell.

Water's still holding in the low-to-mid 70s off the beach, which matters more than people think. That temperature band is exactly why the fluke program is thinning out the way it is. The better grade fish have already staged toward deeper, cooler water ahead of their fall exit — that's a textbook late-September move, not a sign the fishery collapsed. What's left behind in the sod banks off Absecon and up in the Great Egg backwaters is mostly sub-legal fish, fun on light tackle but not filling a cooler. If you're set on fluke this week, work the deeper holes off Longport and the Ocean City reef structure on the last two hours of the outgoing, dragging a 3-inch white Gulp on a 3/4-ounce bucktail slow along bottom. You'll cull through a lot of shorts to find a keeper, and that's the honest read, not a complaint.

Striped bass are where the energy is. The pattern right now is simple and repeatable: find the bunker, find the bass underneath or working the edges. Brigantine beachfront has had bunker pods tight to the second bar on the outgoing tide, and the bass have been sliding in behind them at first light and again in the last hour before dark. A big white or chartreuse bucktail, an ounce and a half, cast past the school and swept through the edge on a slow retrieve has been the move — you don't want to cast into the bait, you want to cast past it and pull your offering out of the pack. Absecon Inlet is holding fish on the jetty rocks on the last two hours of the ebb, when the current funnels bait out past the rock pile. Snag a bunker off the surface with a treble, fish it on a fish-finder rig, free-spool it back into the wash line, and hold on.

Bluefish are riding the same tide. Snapper blues are thick in the back bay creeks behind Ocean City and Sea Isle City right now — small fish, but they're the leading edge of what usually turns into adult blues showing up in the surf zone within a couple weeks. We're already seeing that start along the beachfront, with bunker-fed blitzes breaking sporadically off Ocean City and down toward Townsends Inlet on the outgoing. Diamond jigs, 2 to 3 ounces, or chunked bunker on a fish-finder rig fished right in the wash have both been producing when the blitz windows open. Those windows aren't constant — they're tide-dependent, tight to the last three hours of the ebb when bait gets flushed out and pinched against the beach.

Weakfish are still a back-bay proposition, and a quieter one. Townsends Inlet and the marsh edges up around Stone Harbor have given up decent weakfish after dark on the dropping tide, mullet strips or a 4-inch white Gulp shrimp on a light jighead worked slow along the channel edges. It's not a numbers game right now, more a patient-angler game — one or two quality fish an outing if you put in the time on the right stage of tide.

Kingfish are still around the surf troughs off Ocean City and Sea Isle, bloodworm or Fishbites on a high-low rig fished on the bottom in the cuts between sandbars. Nothing dramatic, but a reliable way to keep a rod bent while you wait on the bigger tide-driven bites to turn on. And for anyone working the inlet rock piles, triggerfish are still holding around the Absecon jetty structure on the last of the incoming, taking clam and squid fished tight to the rocks.

Looking ahead, the moon starts easing off its new-phase peak over the next several days, and that tidal push will soften a bit — expect the blitz windows to shorten rather than disappear entirely. The bunker migration itself isn't going anywhere yet, so predator activity should stay elevated through the week even as the current eases. The bigger story to watch is the mullet run. We haven't seen the real push down the beachfront yet, but once it shows, it typically flips this whole pattern into the fall blitz gear everyone's waiting for. If you've only got one tide to fish this weekend, make it the last two hours of the outgoing at Absecon or Brigantine — that's where the bait, the current, and the bass are lining up right now.
